## Simple explanation

Image classification asks a model to identify what an image shows. It might
label a photograph as a penguin or an ostrich, or assign several tags when
multiple objects or concepts are present.

## Technical explanation

An image classifier maps an input image to scores over a predefined set of
classes. A single-label classifier typically chooses the class with the
highest score; a multi-label classifier can predict several independent
labels. Scores may be logits or probabilities, and the decision rule can
include thresholds or other task-specific logic.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Classification is used for visual search, quality inspection, content
organization, and triage. Production systems also need to account for
uncertain predictions, class imbalance, data shifts, and the cost of different
mistakes.

## How it works

The image is decoded and preprocessed into tensors expected by a model. A
neural network extracts visual features and produces class scores. During
training, the scores are compared with labeled examples using a loss function;
at inference time, the trained model applies a decision rule to new images.

## Practical example

The [Binary Classification notebook](../../notebooks/B/binary-classification.ipynb)
scaffolds a beginner-friendly fast.ai project to classify penguin and ostrich
images. It walks through implementing the model, so the
reader can follow along and learn how to build the classifier.

## Common misconceptions

- A classifier may learn background, image-source, or lighting cues instead
  of the intended object.
- A high accuracy score does not guarantee reliable predictions for every
  class or deployment setting.
- Image classification assigns labels to an image; locating or outlining
  objects requires other tasks such as detection or segmentation.
